label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
Assume GR, SBS, maximality of $\Sigma_1$, and $J<M^2$.
For every fixed $A$ there is $j_*(A)>0$ such that
\[
 M=1,\qquad \overline A\le A,\qquad J<j_*(A)
\]
imply that $(\mathbf E,\mathbf g)$ is isometric to a subextremal Kerr exterior.
head: environment

label: thm:kerr-end
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:kerr-end}
Assume GR, SBS, and maximality of $\Sigma_1$, with $M=1$.
There is a diffeomorphism $\Xi$ from a neighbourhood of spatial
infinity onto a neighbourhood of spatial infinity in the Kerr
metric with mass $1$ and angular momentum $S$ such that
\[
 \Xi^*\mathbf g_{\mathrm{Kerr}}=\mathbf g,\qquad \Xi_*\mathbf T=\partial_t.
\]
head: environment

label: lem:stationary-product
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:stationary-product}
The map
\[
 \Psi:\mathbb R\times\Sigma_1\longrightarrow\mathbf E,
 \qquad \Psi(t,x)=\Psi_{t,\mathbf T}(x)
\]
is a diffeomorphism. In particular $H^1(\mathbf E;\mathbb R)=0$,
and $H_2(\mathbf E;\mathbb R)$ is generated by a large coordinate sphere.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By GR, every stationary orbit meets $\Sigma_1$ transversally,
so $\Psi$ is a surjective local diffeomorphism. We prove that
it is proper and then use achronality to show that the resulting
covering has only one sheet.

Fix a compact set $C\subset\mathbf E$. By the definition of $\mathbf E$
and openness of $\ll$, finitely many open sets $U_i$ cover $C$,
with points $p_i^\pm=(t_i^\pm,x_i^\pm)$ in the asymptotic region satisfying
\[
 p_i^-\ll q\ll p_i^+\qquad(q\in U_i).
\]
Choose $R>\max_i(|t_i^-|+|t_i^+|)$. Timelikeness of the
stationary orbits through $p_i^\pm$ allows us to compare their
large translates with the zero-time slice. Since the flow
preserves $\ll$, for $q\in U_i$ we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stationary-flow-chronology}
 \begin{aligned}
 (0,x_i^-)&\ll\Psi_{s,\mathbf T}(p_i^-)\ll\Psi_{s,\mathbf T}(q),&&s\ge R,\\
 \Psi_{s,\mathbf T}(q)&\ll\Psi_{s,\mathbf T}(p_i^+)\ll(0,x_i^+),&&s\le-R.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Because the zero-time points in
\eqref{eq:stationary-flow-chronology} belong to the achronal
hypersurface $\overline{\Sigma}_1$, no translate
$\Psi_{s,\mathbf T}(C)$ with $|s|\ge R$ can meet that hypersurface.
Consequently, $\Psi(t,x)\in C$ implies $|t|\le R$ and
$x=\Psi_{-t,\mathbf T}(\Psi(t,x))$, whence
\[
 \Psi^{-1}(C)\subset[-R,R]\times
 \left(\Sigma_1\cap
       \{\Psi_{s,\mathbf T}(q):|s|\le R,\ q\in C\}\right).
\]
The set on the right is compact, since $\Sigma_1$ is closed
relative to $\mathbf E$ and the flow image of $[-R,R]\times C$
is compact. As a closed subset of this set, $\Psi^{-1}(C)$
is compact as well, proving properness.

The proper local diffeomorphism $\Psi$ is therefore a covering
of $\mathbf E$, which is connected as the image of
$\mathbb R\times\Sigma_1$. For a point of the asymptotic end,
its entire stationary orbit is timelike, and achronality of
$\overline{\Sigma}_1$ shows that its fiber has exactly one
point. The covering consequently has one sheet, so $\Psi$
is a diffeomorphism.

The cohomology conclusions now follow from
$\mathbf E\simeq\mathbb R\times\Sigma_1$ and
$\Sigma_1\simeq(1,\infty)\times\mathbb S^2$. In particular,
every closed one-form on $\mathbf E$ has a global potential, while
a closed two-form has a global primitive if and only if its
integral over a large coordinate sphere vanishes.
head: environment

label: prop:charging
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:charging}
Under GR, SBS, and the maximal-hypersurface assumption, there are
Lorentz metrics $\mathbf g_q$ and real two-forms $\mathbf F_q$ on
$\mathbf E\cup\mathbf O$, for a neighbourhood $\mathbf O$ of $\mathcal S_0$, such that
\[
 (\mathbf g_1,\mathbf F_1)=(\mathbf g,0),\qquad
 \mathcal L_\mathbf T\mathbf g_q=\mathcal L_\mathbf T\mathbf F_q=0 .
\]
The metrics depend smoothly on $q\in[0,1]$ on every compact subset.
The fields $\mathbf F_q$ are continuous in $q$ and smooth in spacetime.
On $\mathbf E$ the pair
$(\mathbf g_q,\mathbf F_q)$ satisfies \eqref{eq:Einstein-Maxwell} and
\[
 \frac1{4\pi}\int_{S_r}{}^*_{\mathbf g_q}\mathbf F_q=\sqrt{1-q^2},\qquad
 \frac1{4\pi}\int_{S_r}\mathbf F_q=0 .
\]
The fixed fields $\mathbf K,\mathbf Z$ remain Killing near $\mathcal S_0$, and both horizon
branches remain Killing horizons with the same generator $\mathbf K$
and surface gravity. Moreover
$\operatorname{sign}\mathbf g_q(\mathbf T,\mathbf T)=\operatorname{sign}\mathbf g(\mathbf T,\mathbf T)$,
so $\mathbf T$ is timelike in the fixed end.
head: environment

label: prop:end-spheres
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:end-spheres}
Suppose a stationary vacuum end satisfies \eqref{eq:AF},
has $M=1$, and is not Kerr near infinity.
There are $\delta\in(0,1)$ and a smooth family of spacelike
spheres $C_q$, $\delta\le q\le1$, such that
\[
 H_q>|p_q|,\qquad |C_\delta|_{\mathbf g_\delta}<4\pi(1-\delta^2).
\]
Their stationary projections are embedded spheres enclosing a
fixed inner sphere of the end. The family can be chosen in
any sufficiently far end region. If the original end contains
the asymptotic portion of the maximal hypersurface
$\overline\Sigma_1$, then $C_1$ can be joined to a sphere in
$\overline\Sigma_1$ by a path of strictly outward untrapped
spheres in $\mathbf g_1=\mathbf g$ with the same enclosing property.
head: environment

label: prop:band
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:band}
Fix a vacuum spacetime satisfying GR, SBS, and maximality of
$\Sigma_1$, and its normalized Harrison family $\mathbf g_q$.
Let $q:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ and $C_s$ be smooth, with $q(0)=1$
and $C_s$ embedded spacelike spheres in the fixed asymptotic end.
Assume
\[
 \mathbf g_{q(s)}(\mathbf T,\mathbf T)<0\quad\hbox{near }C_s,
 \qquad H_s>|p_s|\quad\hbox{on }C_s.
\]
Suppose $\pi(C_s)$ is embedded and bounds, with $\mathcal S_0$,
a spatial annulus $\mathcal A_s\simeq\mathbb S^2\times[0,1]$.
Assume $C_0\subset\Sigma_1$ bounds a compact truncation of
$\overline\Sigma_1$.
Then this truncation belongs to a smooth family of compact
spacelike hypersurfaces $\Sigma(s)$ such that
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \partial\Sigma(s)=\mathcal S_0\sqcup C_s,\qquad
 \operatorname{tr}_{h_s}k_s=0,\qquad
 \Sigma(s)\simeq\mathbb S^2\times[0,1],\\
 \pi:\Sigma(s)^\circ\longrightarrow\mathcal A_s^\circ
       \quad\text{is a diffeomorphism}.
 \end{gathered}
\]
Here $h_s,k_s$ are the induced metric and second fundamental
form for $\mathbf g_{q(s)}$. Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:area-bound}
 |C_s|_{\mathbf g_{q(s)}}\ge4\pi(1-q(s)^2).
\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose the vacuum end is not Kerr and take the path $C_q$,
$\delta\le q\le1$, supplied by Proposition~\ref{prop:end-spheres}.
To start this path on the original maximal slice, first traverse
the joining path at $q=1$ from the same proposition, and then
follow $C_q$ down to $q=\delta$. After a smooth
reparametrization, Proposition~\ref{prop:band} applies and gives
$|C_\delta|_{\mathbf g_\delta}\ge4\pi(1-\delta^2)$, contradicting
the strict inequality in Proposition~\ref{prop:end-spheres}.

label: lem:optical-completion
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:optical-completion}
A mass-one asymptotically flat stationary vacuum end has a
stationary gauge in which $\overline\mathbf g$ extends analytically
across $\mathbb R\times\{i^0\}$. Here $i^0$ is the point added
to the orbit space. In normal coordinates $y$ for
$\widehat\gamma$ at $i^0$, with $\rho=|y|$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:completion-coordinates}
 \widehat\gamma_{ij}=\delta_{ij}+O(\rho^2),\qquad
 \Omega=\rho^2+O(\rho^3),\qquad
 (\vartheta_0)_i=O(\rho),\qquad y^i(\vartheta_0)_i=0.
\end{equation}
For each remainder $R=O(\rho^k)$ in
\eqref{eq:completion-coordinates}, its normal-coordinate derivatives
satisfy $\partial_y^I R=O(\rho^{k-|I|})$ for every fixed multiindex $I$.
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:optical-normal-data}
 \overline\mathbf g=-\mathrm d\tau^2+\sum_i(\mathrm dy^i)^2+O(\rho).
\end{equation}
head: environment

label: eq:completed-potential-data
title: Proof
body_md:
We use the analytic completion of Beig and Simon~\cite{BeigSimon},
after the stationary regularity improvement of Kennefick and
\'O Murchadha~\cite{KOM}, in the formulation of
\cite{DainInfinity}.
The completed mass and twist potentials of
Geroch and Hansen~\cite{GerochMoments,Hansen} are
\[
 \widehat m=\frac{1-f^2-\psi^2}{4f\sqrt\Omega},\qquad
 \widehat s=\frac{\psi}{2f\sqrt\Omega}.
\]
Together with $\widehat\gamma$ and $\Omega$, they are analytic
at $i^0$ and satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:completed-potential-data}
 \begin{gathered}
 \Omega(i^0)=0,\quad \mathrm d\Omega(i^0)=0,\quad
 \widehat\nabla^2\Omega(i^0)=2\widehat\gamma(i^0),\\
 \widehat m(i^0)=1,\quad \widehat s(i^0)=0,\quad
 \mathrm d\widehat s(i^0)=S_i\,\mathrm dy^i,\qquad
 \widehat m^2+\widehat s^2=1+\Omega.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
Here $\widehat\nabla$ is the connection of $\widehat\gamma$,
and the last derivative follows from the twist expansion
$\psi=2(S\cdot\omega)r^{-2}+O(r^{-3})$ in
\eqref{eq:ernst-end-expansion}.
See also Ace\~na~\cite{Acena} for convergent expansions from
the multipole data. On the punctured end, the definitions and
\eqref{eq:harrison} give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:completed-vacuum-potentials}
 \Phi_0=-\frac{\widehat m+i\widehat s}{\sqrt\Omega},\qquad
 f^{-1}=1+2\Omega+2\widehat m\sqrt\Omega,\qquad
 \psi=2f\widehat s\sqrt\Omega.
\end{equation}
The Hessian normalization in
\eqref{eq:completed-potential-data} gives, in normal coordinates,
$\widehat\gamma_{ij}=\delta_{ij}+O(\rho^2)$ and
$\Omega=\rho^2+O(\rho^3)$. At $q=0$, the transformed twist equation
\eqref{eq:charged-twist} reads
\begin{equation}\label{eq:endpoint-twist}
 f_0^2 *_\gamma\mathrm d\vartheta_0
       =-2\operatorname{Im}(\overline\Phi_0\,\mathrm d\Phi_0).
\end{equation}
Substituting \eqref{eq:harrison} at $q=0$ into
\eqref{eq:endpoint-twist}, we express $\mathrm d\vartheta_0$
in terms of the mass and twist potentials, as in
Dain~\cite{DainInfinity},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:limiting-connection}
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathrm d\vartheta_0
 &=-\tfrac14*_\gamma
       \left(\frac{2\psi}{f}\,\mathrm df
           +\frac{1-f^2+\psi^2}{f^2}\,\mathrm d\psi\right)\\
 &=-2*_{\gamma}\left\{
 \frac{1-f^2-\psi^2}{4f}\,
             \mathrm d\left(\frac\psi{2f}\right)
 -\frac\psi{2f}\,
             \mathrm d\left(\frac{1-f^2-\psi^2}{4f}\right)
                         \right\}\\
 &=-2*_{\gamma}\bigl\{
   \widehat m\sqrt\Omega\,\mathrm d(\widehat s\sqrt\Omega)
  -\widehat s\sqrt\Omega\,\mathrm d(\widehat m\sqrt\Omega)\bigr\}\\
 &=-2\Omega*_{\gamma}
       (\widehat m\,\mathrm d\widehat s
                      -\widehat s\,\mathrm d\widehat m)\\
 &=-2*_{\widehat\gamma}
       (\widehat m\,\mathrm d\widehat s
                      -\widehat s\,\mathrm d\widehat m).
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Here $*_{\gamma}=\Omega^{-1}*_{\widehat\gamma}$ on one-forms.
It follows from the last expression in
\eqref{eq:limiting-connection} that $\mathrm d\vartheta_0$ extends
analytically to the full ball and remains closed there, by
continuity from the punctured ball. We can therefore choose
its radial primitive
\[
 (\vartheta_0)_i(y)
   =\int_0^1 t y^j(\mathrm d\vartheta_0)_{ji}(ty)\,\mathrm dt
\]
which is analytic, is $O(\rho)$, and satisfies
$y^i(\vartheta_0)_i=0$. Since the punctured ball is simply connected,
replacing the original connection by this primitive amounts
to a stationary time change. In this gauge,
\eqref{eq:completion-coordinates} holds and
\eqref{eq:optical-completion} extends analytically across $i^0$.

label: lem:optical-equality
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The inverse Harrison relation \eqref{eq:inverse-harrison}
requires $\Phi_0$ relative to the normalized stationary field
$\partial_\tau$. The Bertotti--Robinson product in
Cl\'ement's construction~\cite{Clement1998} is locally the same
for every $J$, while its stationary field depends on $J$.
We recover that dependence from
$\operatorname{Im}\Phi_0\to-S\cdot\omega$, derived below from
\eqref{eq:completed-potential-data}, and then determine $\Phi_0$
by the Maxwell equations.

Equality of the area with $4\pi$ forces $A=1$ at every point
of the cut, since $A\le1$. By \eqref{eq:integrated-cone-focusing},
we therefore have $\chi=0$ and $\mathbf F_0(L,e_A)=0$ along each
generator from the cut to the vertex. To use these identities
on an open set, translate the cone by the stationary flow.
The geodesics in \eqref{eq:cone-geodesic-data} then give the map
\[
 (u,s,\omega)\longmapsto
 \bigl(u-s+O(s^2),\ s\omega+O(s^2)\bigr),\qquad
 \partial_u=\partial_\tau.
\]
The pullback of $\mathrm d\tau\wedge\mathrm dy^1\wedge
\mathrm dy^2\wedge\mathrm dy^3$ by this map is
$s^2(1+O(s))\,\mathrm du\wedge\mathrm ds\wedge\mathrm d\omega$.
Together with the spatial derivative $I+O(s)$ in $s\omega$,
this shows that $(u,s,\omega)$ are coordinates on a punctured
neighbourhood of the end. In these coordinates the Killing and
affine geodesic equations, followed by the rescaling
$L=-\Omega k$ from \eqref{eq:cone-affine-normalization}, give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:equality-null-normalization}
 \partial_s\overline\mathbf g(\partial_u,k)=0,\qquad
 \overline\mathbf g(\partial_u,k)|_{s=0}=1,
 \qquad \mathbf g_0(\partial_u,\partial_r)=-1.
\end{equation}

Choose the additive constant in $r$ independently of $u$.
Since $\chi=0$ and the angular coordinates are constant
along each ray, the angular metric satisfies the transport
equation with limiting value supplied by \eqref{eq:cone-cut-metric}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:equality-angular-metric}
 \partial_r(\mathbf g_0)_{AB}
       =2\mathbf g_0(\mathbf D^{(0)}_{\partial_A}L,\partial_B)=0,
 \qquad \lim_{r\to\infty}(\mathbf g_0)_{AB}=\overset{\circ}{\gamma}_{AB}.
\end{equation}
Using $\mathbf g_0(\partial_u,\partial_r)=-1$ from
\eqref{eq:equality-null-normalization} and the angular metric
from \eqref{eq:equality-angular-metric}, we write
\begin{equation}\label{eq:equality-metric-Maxwell-form}
 \mathbf g_0=\overset{\circ}{\gamma}-2\,\mathrm du\,\mathrm dr-f_0\,\mathrm du^2
                         +2a_A\,\mathrm du\,\mathrm dx^A.
\end{equation}
Here $a$ is an angular one-form and the coefficients are independent
of $u$. We use the potential to determine $\mathbf F_0$ and fix the
remaining freedom in the affine parameter.
The inversion $y\mapsto y/|y|^2$ and the change from $s$ to
$r$ both reverse orientation, leaving the volume form
$\mathrm du\wedge\mathrm dr\wedge\mathrm d\omega$.
Thus \eqref{eq:charged-potential} and $(\mathbf F_0)_{rA}=0$ give
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \partial_r\operatorname{Im}\Phi_0=({}^*\mathbf F_0)_{ur}
       =\tfrac12(\mathrm d\omega)^{AB}(\mathbf F_0)_{AB},\\
 \mathbf F_0=\mathrm du\wedge\mathrm d\operatorname{Re}\Phi_0
       +(\partial_r\operatorname{Im}\Phi_0)\,\mathrm d\omega.
 \end{gathered}
\]
Here angular indices are raised with $\overset{\circ}{\gamma}$.
The determinant and inverse of \eqref{eq:equality-metric-Maxwell-form}
give $\sqrt{|\det\mathbf g_0|}=\sqrt{\det\overset{\circ}{\gamma}}$,
$(\mathbf F_0)^{ru}=\partial_r\operatorname{Re}\Phi_0$, and
$(\mathbf F_0)^{Au}=0$. The radial Maxwell equations therefore reduce to
\begin{equation}\label{eq:equality-radial-Maxwell}
 \begin{aligned}
 0&=\partial_\mu\bigl(\sqrt{|\det\mathbf g_0|}\,(\mathbf F_0)^{\mu u}\bigr)
       =\sqrt{\det\overset{\circ}{\gamma}}\,\partial_r^2\operatorname{Re}\Phi_0,\\
 0&=(\mathrm d\mathbf F_0)_{rAB}
       =(\partial_r^2\operatorname{Im}\Phi_0)(\mathrm d\omega)_{AB}.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}

The values and derivatives in \eqref{eq:completed-potential-data}
give $\widehat s=S\cdot y+O(\rho^2)$ and
$\widehat m=1+O(\rho^2)$. Formula~\eqref{eq:completed-vacuum-potentials}
therefore gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:equality-potential-limits}
 \frac{\operatorname{Re}\Phi_0}{r}\longrightarrow-1,\qquad
 \operatorname{Im}\Phi_0\longrightarrow-S\cdot\omega.
\end{equation}
Indeed \eqref{eq:cone-geodesic-data} gives $\rho/s\to1$,
and \eqref{eq:cone-affine-asymptotics} gives $rs\to1$
along each ray.
Equations~\eqref{eq:equality-radial-Maxwell} make $\Phi_0$
affine along each ray, and \eqref{eq:equality-potential-limits}
forces $\partial_r\Phi_0=-1$. We may therefore fix the affine
origin by $r=-\operatorname{Re}\Phi_0$. This change is independent
of $u$ and preserves $\partial_r$ and the normalization
\eqref{eq:equality-null-normalization}. It adds multiples of the
null generator to the angular tangents, so it also preserves
the metric \eqref{eq:equality-angular-metric}. We obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:equality-angular-potential}
 \Phi_0=-r+ic,\qquad c=-S\cdot\omega,\qquad
 \mathbf F_0=\mathrm dr\wedge\mathrm du.
\end{equation}
The inverse metric now gives $(\mathbf F_0)^{rA}=a^A$, so the angular
part of $\mathrm dc=i_{\partial_u}{}^*\mathbf F_0$ reads
$\mathrm dc=*_{\overset{\circ}{\gamma}}a$. Applying $*_{\overset{\circ}{\gamma}}^2=-1$, and using
\eqref{eq:harrison} at $q=0$, determines both remaining coefficients,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:equality-endpoint-data}
 a=-*_{\overset{\circ}{\gamma}}\mathrm dc,\qquad
 f_0=|\Phi_0|^2-1=r^2+c^2-1.
\end{equation}

Rotating the angular coordinates so that $S=(0,0,J)$, we have
\[
 c=-J\cos\theta,\qquad
 a=-J\sin^2\theta\,\mathrm d\phi.
\]
Put $R=r+1$ and $\Delta=R^2-2R+J^2$.
Applying the inverse
Harrison relation \eqref{eq:inverse-harrison} to
\eqref{eq:equality-angular-potential}, and extracting the unchanged
orbit metric from \eqref{eq:equality-metric-Maxwell-form}, gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:equality-inverse-data}
 \sigma=\frac{\Phi_0+1}{\Phi_0-1}
          =1-\frac2{R+iJ\cos\theta},\qquad
 \gamma=(\mathrm dr-a)^2+f_0\overset{\circ}{\gamma}.
\end{equation}
Using $f_0=R^2-2R+J^2\cos^2\theta$ and the angular change
$\mathrm d\varphi=\mathrm d\phi+J\Delta^{-1}\mathrm dR$,
we complete the square in \eqref{eq:equality-inverse-data},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:equality-orbit-metric}
 \begin{aligned}
 \gamma
 &=f_0\,\mathrm d\theta^2+\mathrm dR^2
       +2J\sin^2\theta\,\mathrm dR\,\mathrm d\phi
       +\Delta\sin^2\theta\,\mathrm d\phi^2\\
 &=f_0\left(\frac{\mathrm dR^2}{\Delta}
                    +\mathrm d\theta^2\right)
       +\Delta\sin^2\theta
          \left(\mathrm d\phi+\frac J\Delta\mathrm dR\right)^2\\
 &=f_0\left(\frac{\mathrm dR^2}{\Delta}
                    +\mathrm d\theta^2\right)
                  +\Delta\sin^2\theta\,\mathrm d\varphi^2.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Taking real and imaginary parts of the Ernst potential in
\eqref{eq:equality-inverse-data} gives the norm and twist
\begin{equation}\label{eq:equality-vacuum-potentials}
 f=\frac{f_0}{R^2+J^2\cos^2\theta},\qquad
 \psi=\frac{2J\cos\theta}{R^2+J^2\cos^2\theta}.
\end{equation}
Substituting \eqref{eq:equality-vacuum-potentials} into the first
identity in \eqref{eq:stationary-orbit-form-identities}, with the
Hodge star of \eqref{eq:equality-orbit-metric}, determines the
stationary connection through
\begin{equation}\label{eq:equality-vacuum-connection}
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathrm d\left(\frac{2JR\sin^2\theta}{f_0}\,\mathrm d\varphi\right)
 &=\frac{2J\sin\theta}{f_0^2}
   \Bigl[-\sin\theta(R^2-J^2\cos^2\theta)\,\mathrm dR
         \\
 &\hspace{7em}{}+2R\Delta\cos\theta\,\mathrm d\theta\Bigr]
                                      \wedge\mathrm d\varphi\\
 &=f^{-2}\sin\theta\bigl(\psi_\theta\,\mathrm dR
                 -\Delta\psi_R\,\mathrm d\theta\bigr)
                                      \wedge\mathrm d\varphi\\
 &=-f^{-2}*_{\gamma}\mathrm d\psi.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
By \eqref{eq:equality-vacuum-connection}, the difference from
the original vacuum connection is closed and hence exact on
the exterior sphere region. After a stationary time change,
substituting this connection, \eqref{eq:equality-vacuum-potentials},
and \eqref{eq:equality-orbit-metric} into
\eqref{eq:stationary-reduction} gives
\[
 \begin{split}
 \mathbf g={}&-\frac{f_0}{R^2+J^2\cos^2\theta}
       \left(\mathrm dt+\frac{2JR\sin^2\theta}{f_0}
                                      \mathrm d\varphi\right)^2\\
 &+(R^2+J^2\cos^2\theta)
       \left(\frac{\mathrm dR^2}{\Delta}+\mathrm d\theta^2
             +\frac{\Delta\sin^2\theta}{f_0}\,\mathrm d\varphi^2\right).
 \end{split}
\]
This is the Kerr metric with mass one and angular momentum $S$.

label: lem:maximal-compactness
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:maximal-compactness}
Under the hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{prop:band}, let
$s_j\to s_*$ and let $\Sigma_j$ be compact spacelike maximal
stationary graphs with boundary $\mathcal S_0\sqcup C_{s_j}$
and topology $\mathbb S^2\times[0,1]$.
Assume their lapses and stationary heights satisfy
\eqref{eq:lapse-bound} and \eqref{eq:interior-height} uniformly.
Then a subsequence converges smoothly, including at the boundary,
to a compact spacelike maximal stationary graph $\Sigma_*$ with
boundary $\mathcal S_0\sqcup C_{s_*}$ and the same topology.

label: lem:zero-spin-staticity
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:zero-spin-staticity}
Let $\mathbf g$ and $\mathbf T$ be $C^5$ stationary vacuum fields near a spacelike
maximal hypersurface
$\overline\Sigma_1\simeq[1,\infty)\times\mathbb S^2$ with boundary
$\mathcal S_0$. Write $\mathbf T=nT_0+X$, where $T_0$ is the future
unit normal, and $f=-\mathbf g(\mathbf T,\mathbf T)$.
Assume that its end is the zero-time section of
a stationary chart satisfying \eqref{eq:AF} through five
derivatives with $M=1$, that $\mathbf T$ is tangent to $\mathcal S_0$, and
that $n>0$ on $\Sigma_1$. Let $U$ be the component of
$\{f>0\}\cap\Sigma_1$ containing the end and set
$F=\tfrac12\mathrm d\mathbf T^\flat$. If
\begin{equation}\label{eq:staticity-hypotheses}
 \begin{gathered}
 \mathbf T^\flat\wedge F=0\quad\hbox{on }U,\\
 \left.\mathrm df\right|_{T\Sigma_1}\ne0
       \quad\hbox{on }\partial_{\Sigma_1}U,
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
then
\[
 \mathbf T|_{\mathcal S_0}=0,\qquad k=0,\qquad X=0
       \quad\hbox{on }\overline\Sigma_1.
\]
In particular $f=n^2>0$ throughout $\Sigma_1$, and the stationary
metric is static in the region swept out by this slice.
head: environment

label: eq:static-two-form
title: Proof
body_md:
We first prove $\overline U\cap\mathcal S_0\ne\varnothing$.
The $C^5$ fields satisfy \eqref{eq:KID}, with $n=0$ on
$\mathcal S_0$ by tangency of $\mathbf T$ and $n\to1$ at infinity.
The maximum-principle argument proving \eqref{eq:lapse-boundary}
therefore gives $\partial_{\nu_{\mathcal S_0}}n>0$.
On $U$, contracting $\mathbf T^\flat\wedge F=0$ with $\mathbf T$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:static-two-form}
 F=-\frac1{2f}\mathbf T^\flat\wedge\mathrm df,
 \qquad F\wedge F=0\quad\hbox{on }U.
\end{equation}
By continuity, $F\wedge F=0$ also holds on $\overline U$.
Suppose now that $\overline U\cap\mathcal S_0=\varnothing$,
and set $B=\partial_{\Sigma_1}U$. This is a nonempty compact
subset of the open slice, with $f=0$ on $B$. Since $n>0$
there, $\mathbf T$ does not vanish, and the first condition in
\eqref{eq:staticity-hypotheses}, extended by continuity, gives
$F=\mathbf T^\flat\wedge Y$ at each point of $B$. Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:static-zero-level-relations}
 \begin{gathered}
 \mathrm df=2i_\mathbf T F=-2Y(\mathbf T)\mathbf T^\flat,\\
 \mathrm df|_{T\Sigma_1}=-2Y(\mathbf T)X^\flat,
 \qquad |X|_h=n>0\quad\text{on }B.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
The second condition in \eqref{eq:staticity-hypotheses} makes $f$
a local coordinate near $B$. Its positive side belongs to $U$,
so $B$ is a smooth level surface, and
\eqref{eq:static-zero-level-relations} makes $X/n$ its unit normal.
We now compute the flux through this surface. Since
$\operatorname{div}_hX=0$ and $X$ is tangent to $\mathcal S_0$,
\[
 \mathrm d(i_X\mathrm{vol}_h)=(\operatorname{div}_hX)\mathrm{vol}_h=0,
 \qquad \int_{\mathcal S_0} i_X\mathrm{vol}_h=0.
\]
Because $\overline{\Sigma}_1\simeq[1,\infty)\times\mathbb S^2$,
the integral over $\mathcal S_0$ determines the cohomology class
of every closed two-form. The preceding identities therefore
make $i_X\mathrm{vol}_h$ exact, so its flux through each connected
component $B_0$ of $B$ must vanish. But with the unit normal $X/n$
from \eqref{eq:static-zero-level-relations}, this says
\[
 0=\int_{B_0}i_X\mathrm{vol}_h=\int_{B_0}n\,\mathrm d A>0,
\]
a contradiction. Hence there is a point
$p\in\overline U\cap\mathcal S_0$.

We use the point $p$ to prove that $X$ vanishes on the whole
sphere. Its restriction is Killing, since $n=0$ and
$\mathcal L_Xh=2nk$ imply $\mathcal L_X(h|_{T\mathcal S_0})=0$, and
$p\in\overline U$ together with $f|_{\mathcal S_0}=-|X|^2$
gives $X(p)=0$. It remains to show that its tangential derivative
at $p$, a rotation with coefficient $\omega_p$, also vanishes.
The flow of $\mathbf T$ fixes $p$ and preserves $\mathcal S_0$, so its
derivative preserves both the tangent and normal planes.
Since $n=X=0$ at $p$,
\[
 \mathbf g(\mathbf D_{\nu_{\mathcal S_0}}\mathbf T,T_0)
       =-\partial_{\nu_{\mathcal S_0}}n.
\]
Preservation of the normal plane and the Killing equation give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:static-normal-boost}
 \mathbf D_{\nu_{\mathcal S_0}}\mathbf T
       =(\partial_{\nu_{\mathcal S_0}}n)T_0,
 \qquad
 \mathbf D_{T_0}\mathbf T
       =(\partial_{\nu_{\mathcal S_0}}n)\nu_{\mathcal S_0}.
\end{equation}
The normal derivatives in \eqref{eq:static-normal-boost} and the
tangential rotation give, in an adapted orthonormal coframe,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:static-boundary-wedge}
 \begin{aligned}
 F|_p&=(\partial_{\nu_{\mathcal S_0}}n)\,
                   \theta^0\wedge\theta^1
                  +\omega_p\,\theta^2\wedge\theta^3,\\
 (F\wedge F)|_p
   &=2\omega_p(\partial_{\nu_{\mathcal S_0}}n)\,
                   \theta^0\wedge\theta^1\wedge\theta^2\wedge\theta^3
     =0.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The vanishing of $F\wedge F$ on $\overline U$ from
\eqref{eq:static-two-form}, together with the positive normal
lapse derivative in \eqref{eq:lapse-boundary}, forces
$\omega_p=0$ in \eqref{eq:static-boundary-wedge}. Thus the
Killing field $X|_{\mathcal S_0}$ and its derivative vanish at
$p$. Restricting it to geodesics gives Jacobi fields with zero
initial data, so it vanishes on the connected sphere and
$\mathbf T|_{\mathcal S_0}=0$.

We integrate the Sudarsky--Wald identity
\eqref{eq:stationary-divergence}. On $S_R=\{r=R\}$, with outward
unit normal $\nu_R$, the decay $k=O(r^{-3})$, $X=O(r^{-2})$
from \eqref{eq:slice-asymptotic-data} makes the flux tend to zero.
Since $X=0$ on $\mathcal S_0$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:staticity-integral}
 \begin{aligned}
 \int_{\Sigma_1}n|k|^2\,\mathrm d\mu_h
   &=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{S_R}k(X,\nu_R)\,\mathrm d A\\
   &\quad-\int_{\mathcal S_0}k(X,\nu_{\mathcal S_0})\,\mathrm d A=0.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Since $n>0$, \eqref{eq:staticity-integral} gives $k=0$, and
\eqref{eq:KID} makes $X$ Killing on the slice. Its tangential
derivatives vanish on $\mathcal S_0$, and the Killing equation
then gives the normal derivative as well. The same uniqueness
argument along geodesics gives $X=0$ on the connected slice.
Thus $\mathbf T=nT_0$ and $f=n^2>0$, and the stationary translates of
the slice are orthogonal to $\mathbf T$.

label: eq:small-spin-contradiction
title: Proof
body_md:
We prove \eqref{eq:horizon-smallness}. If this estimate has no
positive threshold $j_*(A)$ for a fixed $A$, there are smooth
spacetimes $(\mathbf g_j,\mathbf T_j,\Sigma_{1,j})$ satisfying the hypotheses with
$M_j=1$ and $\overline A_j\le A$, and angular momenta $S_j$ of
magnitude $J_j=|S_j|$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:small-spin-contradiction}
 J_j\longrightarrow0,\qquad
 \sup_{\mathcal S_0}\mathbf g_j(\mathbf T_j,\mathbf T_j)
             \ge\varepsilon_{\mathrm{AIK}}(A)^2>0.
\end{equation}
Pull back the fields by the charts of Section~\ref{subsec:assumptions}.
To retain a Lorentzian limit, we need a uniform bound for the
inverse metric. Suppress $j$ and let $h^{ij}$ denote the inverse of the spatial block
$\mathbf g_{ij}$ in these coordinates. The bounds for $h$ at
$t=0$ and for $\partial_t\mathbf g_{ij}$ in
Section~\ref{subsec:assumptions} keep $\mathbf g_{ij}$ uniformly positive
definite after decreasing the time interval uniformly in $j$. We restrict this strip to
$r>3/4$. The time-coordinate estimate \eqref{eq:coordinate-time-bound}
and $R_1\ge A_1^4$ give $-\mathbf g_{00}\ge c(A)>0$.
Putting $a^2=-\mathbf g_{00}+h^{ij}\mathbf g_{0i}\mathbf g_{0j}\ge c(A)$,
block inversion gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:coordinate-inverse-bounds}
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathbf g^{00}&=-a^{-2},\qquad
 \mathbf g^{0i}=a^{-2}h^{ij}\mathbf g_{0j},\\
 \mathbf g^{ij}&=h^{ij}-a^{-2}h^{ik}\mathbf g_{0k}h^{j\ell}\mathbf g_{0\ell}.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The inverse metric is therefore uniformly bounded, and
repeated differentiation of $\mathbf g^{-1}\mathbf g=\operatorname{Id}$,
starting with $\partial\mathbf g^{-1}=-\mathbf g^{-1}(\partial\mathbf g)\mathbf g^{-1}$,
gives the same control through six derivatives by
\eqref{eq:effective-bound}. We can thus apply Arzel\`a--Ascoli and
pass to a diagonal subsequence for which
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stationary-compactness}
 \begin{gathered}
 \mathbf g_j\longrightarrow \mathbf g,\qquad \mathbf T_j\longrightarrow \mathbf T
        \quad\text{in }C^{5,\alpha}(K)\\
        \quad\text{for every compact }K,\qquad 0<\alpha<1.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
The bound for $\mathbf g_j^{-1}$ keeps $\mathbf g$ Lorentzian, and
\eqref{eq:stationary-compactness} passes the vacuum and Killing
equations, tangency to $\mathcal S_0$, and \eqref{eq:KID} to
the limit. We use $\mathbf g,\mathbf T,h,k,n,X$ for the limiting fields
from now on. To identify their mass and angular momentum, we
retain the uniform remainders in \eqref{eq:AF}, which give,
for $|I|\le5$,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |\partial^I(\mathbf g_{00,j}+1-2/r)|&\le C_Ir^{-2-|I|},\\
 |\partial^I(\mathbf g_{0i,j}+2\epsilon_{iak}S_j^a x^kr^{-3})|
                                      &\le C_Ir^{-3-|I|}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Passing to the limit at each fixed point of the end, using
\eqref{eq:stationary-compactness} and $J_j\to0$, yields
$\mathbf g_{00}=-1+2/r+O_5(r^{-2})$ and $\mathbf g_{0i}=O_5(r^{-3})$,
so the limiting fields have $M=1$ and $J=0$. The lapse bound
\eqref{eq:lapse-boundary} also passes to the limit, with
$0\le n\le1$ and $n=0$ on $\mathcal S_0$. Since the retained
asymptotics give $n\to1$ at infinity, the strong maximum
principle applied to the limiting equation in \eqref{eq:KID}
gives $0<n<1$ in the interior, and hence
$f=n^2-|X|^2<1$.

Let $U_j$ and $U$ be the components containing the end of
$\{f_j>0\}\cap\Sigma_{1,j}$ and $\{f>0\}\cap\Sigma_1$,
respectively. Given a smooth curve $c:[0,1]\to U$, choose a point
$x_*$ in the common timelike asymptotic end and join it to
$c(0)$ by a compact path in $U$. Since $f$ has a
positive minimum on the union of this path and $c$,
\eqref{eq:stationary-compactness} places the union in
$\{f_j>0\}$ for large $j$, and hence in $U_j$. In particular,
\eqref{eq:twist-smallness} gives $\psi_j\to0$ throughout $U$,
so $\sigma_j=f_j+i\psi_j\to f$ there.

To identify the limiting twist, set $F_j=\tfrac12\mathrm d\mathbf T_j^\flat$
and $F=\tfrac12\mathrm d\mathbf T^\flat$. By \eqref{eq:stationary-compactness},
\eqref{eq:vacuum-ernst}, and \eqref{eq:twist-smallness},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:limiting-twist-zero}
 \begin{aligned}
 \int_c2i_\mathbf T{}^*_{\mathbf g}F
 &=\lim_{j\to\infty}\int_c2i_{\mathbf T_j}{}^*_{\mathbf g_j}F_j\\
 &=\lim_{j\to\infty}\bigl[\psi_j(c(1))-\psi_j(c(0))\bigr]=0.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
As $c$ is arbitrary, \eqref{eq:limiting-twist-zero} shows that
$2i_\mathbf T{}^*_{\mathbf g}F$ vanishes on $T\Sigma_1$ over $U$. It also
annihilates $\mathbf T$, which is timelike on $U$ and therefore
transverse to the spacelike slice. Thus $i_\mathbf T{}^*_{\mathbf g}F=0$
there, or equivalently $\mathbf T^\flat\wedge F=0$.

With $\mathcal F=F+i{}^*_{\mathbf g}F$, we can now pass to the second identity
of \eqref{eq:Kerr-identities}, using
\eqref{eq:stationary-compactness} and $\sigma_j\to f$. On $U$
we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Schwarz-self-dual-limit}
 \mathcal F^2=-\frac{(1-f)^4}{4},\qquad
 \mathcal F^2=2\bigl(F_{\alpha\beta}F^{\alpha\beta}
               +iF_{\alpha\beta}({}^*F)^{\alpha\beta}\bigr).
\end{equation}
Taking real parts in \eqref{eq:Schwarz-self-dual-limit} and using continuity gives
$F_{\alpha\beta}F^{\alpha\beta}=-(1-f)^4/8$ on $\overline U$.
At an interior boundary point of $U$, we have $f=0$ and $n>0$,
so $\mathbf T$ is nonzero and null. The vanishing twist therefore gives
$F=\mathbf T^\flat\wedge Y$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Schwarz-identities}
 \begin{gathered}
 F_{\alpha\beta}F^{\alpha\beta}=-2Y(\mathbf T)^2=-\tfrac18,
 \qquad \mathrm df=-2Y(\mathbf T)\mathbf T^\flat,\\
 |\mathrm df|_h^2=4Y(\mathbf T)^2|X|_h^2
       =-2F_{\alpha\beta}F^{\alpha\beta}n^2
       =\tfrac14 n^2>0.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
Equation~\eqref{eq:Schwarz-identities} verifies the remaining
condition in \eqref{eq:staticity-hypotheses}, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:zero-spin-staticity}, with the lapse, asymptotics,
and boundary conditions already verified, gives $\mathbf T|_{\mathcal S_0}=0$.
Restricting \eqref{eq:stationary-compactness} to $\mathcal S_0$ gives
$\sup_{\mathcal S_0}\mathbf g_j(\mathbf T_j,\mathbf T_j)\to0$.
This contradicts \eqref{eq:small-spin-contradiction}, proving
\eqref{eq:horizon-smallness} for some $j_*(A)>0$. The Kerr
conclusion follows from
the global rigidity theorem of~\cite{AIKsmall},
with the same effective constant $A$.

label: lem:harrison-collar
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:harrison-collar}
For each $q\in[0,1]$, there is an outward unit spacelike normal
field along $\mathcal S_0$ whose geodesics form a spacelike
exterior collar, parametrized by length $\rho$ and base point $y$.
This collar meets each $\mathbf T$-orbit through
it once. Its $\mathbf K$-translates have coordinates $(t,\rho,y)$ with
$0<\rho<\rho_0$, in which
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ADM-collar}
 \begin{gathered}
 \mathbf g_q=\mathrm d\rho^2+
 (h_\rho)_{AB}(\mathrm dy^A+\beta^A\mathrm dt)
                    (\mathrm dy^B+\beta^B\mathrm dt)-a^2\mathrm dt^2,\\
 \partial_t=\mathbf K,\qquad -\infty<t<\infty .
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
The slices $t=\mathrm{const}$ are spacelike, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:collar-orders}
 \begin{gathered}
 a=\kappa\rho+O(\rho^3),\qquad
 \beta=O(\rho^2),\qquad \partial_\rho\beta=O(\rho),\\
 h_\rho=h_0+O(\rho^2),\qquad
 \partial_\rho h_\rho=O(\rho).
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
Here $\mathbf T(\rho)=0$ and, at $q=1$, the restriction of $\rho$ to
$\overline\Sigma_1$ is a smooth defining function of $\mathcal S_0$.
Regular normal coordinates $(x^0,x^1,y)$ extend across the sphere.
On the exterior part of their neighbourhood they satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:collar-boost-coordinates}
 x^0=\rho\sinh(\kappa t),\qquad
 x^1=\rho\cosh(\kappa t).
\end{equation}
Here $\partial_{x^0},\partial_{x^1}$ form an orthonormal normal
frame on $\mathcal S_0$, with $\partial_{x^0}$ future timelike.
The regular coordinates and the coefficients in
\eqref{eq:ADM-collar} depend smoothly on $q$, with differentiated
remainder bounds uniform for $q\in[0,1]$.

label: lem:temporal-gradient
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:temporal-gradient}
Let $\mathbf g_j$ be smooth Lorentz metrics converging in $C^2$ to a
Lorentz metric near a fixed compact set $Q$.
Let $\tau$ be a fixed smooth function with
past timelike gradient and
\[
 \alpha_j^2=-\mathbf g_j^{-1}(\mathrm d\tau,\mathrm d\tau)\ge a_0^2>0
       \quad\hbox{on }Q\cap\{\tau\ge0\}.
\]
Suppose $\Sigma_j$ are smooth spacelike maximal hypersurfaces
with future unit normals $T_{0,j}$, whose portions $\Sigma_j\cap\{\tau\ge0\}$ are compact and
contained in $Q$. Put
\[
 V_j=-\alpha_j^{-1}\operatorname{grad}_{\mathbf g_j}\tau,
 \qquad v_j=-\mathbf g_j(T_{0,j},V_j),
 \qquad \tau_{\max}=\max_Q\max(\tau,0).
\]
There is an exponent $\mu>4$, depending only on $a_0$,
$\sup_j(\|\mathbf g_j\|_{C^2(Q)}+\|\mathbf g_j^{-1}\|_{C^0(Q)})$, and
$\|\tau\|_{C^3(Q)}$ in a fixed finite coordinate cover, such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:temporal-gradient}
 \sup_{\Sigma_j\cap\{\tau>0\}}\tau^\mu v_j
 \le2\max\left\{2\tau_{\max}^\mu,
       \sup_{\partial\Sigma_j\cap\{\tau>0\}}\tau^\mu v_j\right\}.
\end{equation}
The boundary supremum is zero when its set is empty.

label: prop:compact-causal
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{prop:compact-causal}
Let $\mathbf g$ be a $C^2$ time-oriented Lorentz metric on
$\mathcal B$. Suppose that every compact $C\subset\mathcal B$
admits a constant $L_C$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:compact-proper-time}
 L_\mathbf g(c)\le L_C
\end{equation}
for every Lipschitz future curve $c:[a,b]\to C$ with
$\mathbf g(\dot c,\dot c)\le-\epsilon_c<0$ almost everywhere.
Then every compact $Q\Subset\mathcal B$ has a neighbourhood
admitting a smooth function with past timelike gradient.

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $\mathbf g_j=\mathbf g_{q(s_j)}$ and $n_j=-\mathbf g_j(\mathbf T,T_{0,j})$.
The estimate \eqref{eq:outer-collar-normal} bounds the normals
on a fixed outer collar.

At a fixed small $\rho_0>0$, smooth parameter dependence in
Lemma~\ref{lem:harrison-collar} and
\eqref{eq:charged-boost-expansions} place the zero-time collar
spheres and their $\mathbf Z$-orbits in a common compact subset of
$\mathbf E$, with stationary projections in one compact interior
annulus. Consequently \eqref{eq:interior-height} bounds $G_j$
on this set, and \eqref{eq:corotating-graph} bounds the corotating
heights $v_j(\rho_0,\cdot)$ on both sides. Applying
\eqref{eq:collar-height} to each fixed hypersurface gives this
uniform bound throughout the collar and hence \eqref{eq:wedge}.

In the regular normal coordinates of
Lemma~\ref{lem:harrison-collar}, the coefficients converge smoothly
and $-\mathbf g_j(\partial_{x^0},\partial_{x^0})\ge1/2$ on a common
smaller neighbourhood. The corotating graphs $t=v_j(\rho,y)$
satisfy $|x^0|\le\theta x^1$ by \eqref{eq:wedge}, while
\eqref{eq:collar-boost-coordinates} gives $x^1\ge\rho$.
Along each angular ray, the derivative of $x^1$ cannot vanish,
since the tangent would then be
a nonzero multiple of the timelike field $\partial_{x^0}$,
and it is positive because $x^1\to0$ as $\rho\downarrow0$.
Thus the hypersurfaces are graphs $x^0=w_j(z)$, $z=(x^1,y)$,
on a common half-cylinder. The inequality
$|w_j|\le\theta x^1$ gives at $x^1=0$
\begin{equation}\label{eq:horizon-boundary-normal}
 \begin{gathered}
 w_j=0,\qquad \partial_yw_j=0,\qquad
 |\partial_{x^1}w_j|\le\theta<1,\\
 -\mathbf g_j(T_{0,j},\partial_{x^0})
       \le(1-\theta^2)^{-1/2}.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}

To extend the normal bound from $\mathcal S_0$ into the collar, choose
$\theta<c<1$ and angular coordinates orthonormal at a fixed
point of $\mathcal S_0$. On a sufficiently small coordinate
half-ball $|z|<r_0$ put
\[
 \delta=\frac{(c-\theta)r_0}{4},\qquad
 \epsilon=\frac\delta{4c},\qquad
 \tau=\delta+x^0-c\sqrt{\epsilon^2+|z|^2}.
\]
For the constant Minkowski form,
$(\partial_{x^0}\tau)^2-|\partial_z\tau|^2\ge1-c^2$.
Shrinking the chart and using smooth metric convergence, together
with $|w_j|\le\theta|z|$ on the hypersurfaces, gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:horizon-temporal-cutoff}
 \begin{gathered}
 -\mathbf g_j^{-1}(\mathrm d\tau,\mathrm d\tau)\ge(1-c^2)/2,\\
 \tau\le-\tfrac34(c-\theta)r_0\quad\hbox{when }|z|=r_0,\\
 \tau\ge\delta/2\quad\hbox{when }
       |z|\le\delta/[4(c+\theta)].
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
The parameters $r_0,\epsilon$ fix the $C^3$ bound for $\tau$.
With $V_j,\alpha_j$ as in Lemma~\ref{lem:temporal-gradient},
$\partial_{x^0}\tau=1$ gives
\[
 -\mathbf g_j\left(V_j,
       \frac{\partial_{x^0}}{\sqrt{-\mathbf g_{j,00}}}\right)
       =\frac1{\alpha_j\sqrt{-\mathbf g_{j,00}}}\le C.
\]
Here \eqref{eq:horizon-temporal-cutoff} bounds $\alpha_j$ below,
and $-\mathbf g_{j,00}\ge1/2$. The same cutoff excludes $|z|=r_0$
from $\{\tau>0\}$, while this angle bound and
\eqref{eq:horizon-boundary-normal} control the boundary term
in Lemma~\ref{lem:temporal-gradient}. The lemma bounds the
normals where $\tau\ge\delta/2$, and a finite cover of
$\mathcal S_0$ gives a fixed collar with bounded normals.

A normal bound gives ellipticity of the graph equation in
both boundary and interior charts. For a local graph $x^0=w(z)$ with timelike
vertical field, set
\[
 e_a=\partial_{z^a}+p_a\partial_{x^0},\qquad
 h_{ab}=\mathbf g_j(e_a,e_b),\qquad
 L_j(z,w,p)=\sqrt{\det h}.
\]
At $(w,p)=(w_j,\mathrm dw_j)$, maximality and differentiation
of the volume density give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:maximal-graph-ellipticity}
 \begin{gathered}
 -\partial_aL_{j,p_a}+L_{j,w}=0,\\
 L_{j,p_a}=L_jh^{ab}\mathbf g_j(\partial_{x^0},e_b),\\
 \begin{aligned}
 -L_{j,p_ap_b}
 &=L_jh^{ab}\bigl[h^{cd}\mathbf g_j(\partial_{x^0},e_c)
                       \mathbf g_j(\partial_{x^0},e_d)-\mathbf g_{j,00}\bigr]\\
 &=L_jh^{ab}[\mathbf g_j(\partial_{x^0},T_{0,j})]^2,
 \end{aligned}\\
 \det h=-\det\mathbf g_j/[\mathbf g_j(\partial_{x^0},T_{0,j})]^2.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
To obtain uniform ellipticity from
\eqref{eq:maximal-graph-ellipticity}, use the metric bounds and
$\mathbf g_{j,00}\le-c<0$ to obtain
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 0<h_{aa}=\mathbf g_{j,aa}+2p_a\mathbf g_{j,0a}+p_a^2\mathbf g_{j,00}
       \le C(1+|p_a|)-cp_a^2,\\
 |p|\le C,\qquad h\le C\operatorname{Id}.
 \end{gathered}
\]
The normal bound, reverse Cauchy--Schwarz inequality, and
nondegeneracy of the ambient metric then give
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 c\le-\mathbf g_{j,00}\le[\mathbf g_j(\partial_{x^0},T_{0,j})]^2\le C,\\
 c\le\det h=-\frac{\det\mathbf g_j}
                  {[\mathbf g_j(\partial_{x^0},T_{0,j})]^2}\le C,
 \qquad \lambda_{\min}(h)\ge C^{-2}\det h\ge c.
 \end{gathered}
\]
Substitution in the Hessian formula
\eqref{eq:maximal-graph-ellipticity} yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:graph-elliptic-bounds}
 \lambda|\xi|^2\le-L_{j,p_ap_b}\xi_a\xi_b\le\Lambda|\xi|^2
\end{equation}
with constants independent of $j$. Smooth convergence of
$\mathbf g_j$ gives bounds for every fixed number of derivatives of
$L_j$ on these compact sets of $(z,w,p)$. At the horizon the
Dirichlet data are $w_j=0$ by \eqref{eq:horizon-boundary-normal}.
The bound \eqref{eq:graph-elliptic-bounds}, boundary
$C^{1,\alpha}$ estimates, and Schauder estimates therefore give
uniform $C^{m,\alpha}$ bounds for each $m\ge2$ on smaller
half-balls. At the outer boundary, smooth convergence of
$C_{s_j}$ gives bounded Dirichlet data and bounded boundary
straightening maps, so the same estimates apply there.

We next bound the interior normals. Identify the moving annuli
by smooth stationary diffeomorphisms and write
$\mathcal B=\mathbb R\times\mathcal A^\circ$ for their common
stationary region, with limiting metric $\mathbf g_*$.
Fix a Lipschitz future $\mathbf g_*$-timelike segment $c$ in a compact
set $Q$, with $\mathbf g_*(\dot c,\dot c)\le-\epsilon_c<0$ almost
everywhere. Its bounded tangent and metric convergence keep it
$\mathbf g_j$-timelike for large $j$. The reverse Cauchy--Schwarz
inequality, \eqref{eq:translated-graph-time}, and the height bound
\eqref{eq:interior-height} give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:limit-proper-time}
 \begin{aligned}
 L_{\mathbf g_*}(c)=\lim_jL_{\mathbf g_j}(c)
 &\le C\limsup_j\bigl[G_j(c_+)-G_j(c_-)\bigr]\\
 &\le C\bigl(\operatorname{osc}_Q t+2C_{\pi(Q)}\bigr).
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Here the chain rule for $G_j=t-u_j(x)$ holds almost everywhere.
Thus \eqref{eq:compact-proper-time} holds for $\mathbf g_*$. Choose a compact
spatial annulus $K\Subset\mathcal A^\circ$ whose boundary lies
in the collars with bounded normals. Its truncated hypersurfaces
\[
 M_j=\Sigma_j\cap\pi^{-1}(K)
       \subset Q=[-C_K,C_K]\times K
\]
have bounded boundary normals. Lemma~\ref{prop:compact-causal}
supplies a fixed temporal function $\tau$ near $Q$, which we
shift so that $1\le\tau\le\tau_{\max}$. Compactness and convergence
of the inverse metrics give, for large $j$,
\[
 \inf_Q[-\mathbf g_j^{-1}(\mathrm d\tau,\mathrm d\tau)]
 \ge\tfrac12\min_Q[-\mathbf g_*^{-1}(\mathrm d\tau,\mathrm d\tau)]>0.
\]
This bound, the fixed $C^3$ norm of $\tau$, and smooth convergence
of $\mathbf g_j$ control the coefficients in
Lemma~\ref{lem:temporal-gradient}, whose boundary term is
controlled by the collar estimates. Equation~\eqref{eq:temporal-gradient}
therefore bounds the interior normals.

All hypersurfaces now lie in a fixed compact region and have
uniformly bounded normals. In a sufficiently small cylinder
with timelike vertical field, each is a graph over a fixed
spatial ball. To verify that the graph has a uniform domain,
let $L$ bound its coordinate slope and choose the cylinder
$(-4Lr,4Lr)\times B_{4r}$. Starting at a point near its centre,
continuation along radial segments over $B_r$ satisfies
\[
 |w_j(y)|\le|w_j(y_j)|+L|y-y_j|\le2Lr.
\]
Thus the graph cannot reach $x^0=\pm4Lr$ and continues
at any interior endpoint by closedness of the hypersurface
and transversality to $\partial_{x^0}$. It is the only sheet
in a smaller cylinder, since $G_j$ has timelike gradient and
therefore increases strictly along each entire vertical fiber.
We may consequently apply the ellipticity bound
\eqref{eq:graph-elliptic-bounds} on a fixed domain, obtaining
uniform $C^{m,\alpha}$ estimates on smaller balls.

Choose a Hausdorff convergent subsequence in the common compact
region. The graph estimates upgrade its convergence to smooth
convergence near interior limit points, and the collar estimates
give the same conclusion at the boundary. Uniqueness on vertical
fibers prevents crossing sheets or coincident sheets with
multiplicity, so these local limits agree to form a smooth
compact connected spacelike maximal hypersurface $\Sigma_*$,
with $\partial\Sigma_*=\mathcal S_0\sqcup C_{s_*}$.

It remains to show that $\Sigma_*^\circ$ meets each stationary
orbit in $\mathcal B$ exactly once.
Passing \eqref{eq:charged-lapse-equation} to the smooth limit gives
\[
 n_*\ge0,\qquad
 \Delta_{\Sigma_*}n_*
   =\bigl(|k_*|^2+\mathbf R_*(T_{0,*},T_{0,*})\bigr)n_*.
\]
The nonnegative coefficient in \eqref{eq:charged-constraint}
and the strict outer-collar bound
$n_*\ge\sqrt{-\mathbf g_*(\mathbf T,\mathbf T)}>0$ allow us to apply the strong
maximum principle. We obtain $n_*>0$ on the connected interior,
so the stationary projection is a local diffeomorphism.
It is also bijective. For each fixed $x$, boundedness of
$u_j(x)$ gives a limit point above $x$, while two such points
would, by transversality and smooth local convergence, produce
two points of each late graph above $x$. Hence
$\Sigma_*^\circ=\{t=u_*(x)\}$.

To identify the topology of the limit, straighten
$C_{s_j}$ to $C_{s_*}$ by diffeomorphisms tending to the identity
and fixing $\mathcal S_0$. Smooth convergence up to both
boundary collars then makes normal projection onto $\Sigma_*$
a diffeomorphism for large $j$, proving
$\Sigma_*\simeq\mathbb S^2\times[0,1]$.

label: eq:tilt-derivatives
title: Proof
body_md:
Suppress $j$. We estimate $v=-\mathbf g(T_0,V)$ by differentiating
along $\Sigma$, keeping the terms containing its second
fundamental form explicit. The remaining coefficients are
bounded by the hypotheses, since
$V=-\alpha^{-1}\operatorname{grad}_{\mathbf g}\tau$ and $\alpha\ge a_0$
give bounds for $V,\mathbf D V,\mathbf D^2V$ and $\operatorname{Ric}(\mathbf g)$ in the fixed
coordinate cover. Choose a tangent orthonormal frame with
$\nabla_{e_a}e_b=0$ at the point, put $V^a=\mathbf g(V,e_a)$, and note that
$v^2=1+\alpha^{-2}|\nabla_\Sigma\tau|^2$.
The Gauss formula $\mathbf D_{e_a}e_b=-k_{ab}T_0$ and
$\operatorname{tr}k=0$ give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tilt-derivatives}
 \begin{aligned}
 \nabla_a v&=k_{ab}V^b-\mathbf g(T_0,\mathbf D_{e_a}V),\\
 \nabla_aV^b&=\mathbf g(\mathbf D_{e_a}V,e_b)+vk_{ab},\\
 \Delta_\Sigma v
 &=(\nabla^ak_{ab})V^b
       +k^{ab}\bigl[\mathbf g(\mathbf D_{e_a}V,e_b)+vk_{ab}\bigr]\\
 &\quad+k^{ab}\mathbf g(e_b,\mathbf D_{e_a}V)
       -\mathbf g\left(T_0,\sum_a(\mathbf D^2V)(e_a,e_a)\right)\\
 &=|k|^2v+(\nabla^ak_{ab})V^b
       +2k^{ab}\mathbf g(e_b,\mathbf D_{e_a}V)\\
 &\qquad-\mathbf g\left(T_0,\sum_a(\mathbf D^2V)(e_a,e_a)\right).
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
In an ambient orthonormal frame with time axis $V$, the
components of $T_0,e_a$ are bounded by $Cv$.
Using Codazzi and the ambient Ricci bound in
\eqref{eq:tilt-derivatives} gives, for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$,
\[
 \Delta_\Sigma v
 \ge |k|^2v-C|k|v^2-Cv^3
 \ge(1-\varepsilon)|k|^2v-C_\varepsilon v^3.
\]
For $\eta=\operatorname{arcosh}v$ on $\{v>2\}$, this yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tilt-laplacian}
 \begin{aligned}
 \Delta_\Sigma\eta
 &=\coth\eta\left(\frac{\Delta_\Sigma v}{v}
                           -|\nabla_\Sigma\eta|^2\right)\\
 &\ge\coth\eta\bigl\{
 (1-\varepsilon)|k|^2-|\nabla_\Sigma\eta|^2
                                  -C_\varepsilon v^2\bigr\}.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
To retain a positive gradient term, let $\lambda_1$ be the
eigenvalue of $k$ of greatest absolute value. Maximality gives
\[
 |k|^2\ge\lambda_1^2+\tfrac12(\lambda_2+\lambda_3)^2
          =\tfrac32\lambda_1^2.
\]
The first identity in \eqref{eq:tilt-derivatives} and
$\sum_a(V^a)^2=v^2-1$ give, for fixed $\varepsilon>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tilt-gradient-control}
 \begin{aligned}
 |\nabla_\Sigma\eta|
 &\le\frac{|k_{ab}V^b|+Cv^2}{\sqrt{v^2-1}}
       \le|\lambda_1|+Cv,\\
 |\nabla_\Sigma\eta|^2
 &\le(1+\varepsilon)\lambda_1^2+C_\varepsilon v^2
       \le\tfrac23(1+\varepsilon)|k|^2+C_\varepsilon v^2.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Fix $0<\varepsilon\le1/11$. Substituting
\eqref{eq:tilt-gradient-control} in
\eqref{eq:tilt-laplacian} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:coercive-tilt}
 \begin{gathered}
 \begin{aligned}
 \Delta_\Sigma\eta
 &\ge\coth\eta\left\{
   \left[\frac{3(1-\varepsilon)}{2(1+\varepsilon)}-1\right]
        |\nabla_\Sigma\eta|^2-C_\varepsilon v^2\right\}\\
 &\ge\coth\eta
       \bigl\{\tfrac14|\nabla_\Sigma\eta|^2-Cv^2\bigr\},
 \end{aligned}\\
 |\Delta_\Sigma\tau|
       =|\operatorname{tr}_{T\Sigma}\mathbf D^2\tau|\le Cv^2.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
At an interior maximum of $\eta+\mu\log\tau$,
\[
 \nabla_\Sigma\eta=-\frac\mu\tau\nabla_\Sigma\tau.
\]
Using both bounds in \eqref{eq:coercive-tilt}, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:weighted-tilt}
 \begin{aligned}
 0&\ge\Delta_\Sigma\eta+\frac\mu\tau\Delta_\Sigma\tau
                  -\frac\mu{\tau^2}|\nabla_\Sigma\tau|^2\\
  &\ge\coth\eta\left\{
    \frac{\mu^2/4-\mu\tanh\eta}{\tau^2}
                     |\nabla_\Sigma\tau|^2
       -Cv^2\left(1+\frac{\mu\tanh\eta}{\tau}\right)\right\}\\
  &\ge\coth\eta\left\{
    \frac{\mu^2/4-\mu}{\tau^2}|\nabla_\Sigma\tau|^2
       -Cv^2\left(1+\frac\mu\tau\right)\right\}.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The positive coefficient in \eqref{eq:weighted-tilt} is quadratic
in $\mu$, while the error is linear, with $C$ independent of
$\mu$ and the hypersurface. Choose $\mu$ sufficiently large that
\[
 (\mu^2/4-\mu)a_0^2
       \ge2C(\tau_{\max}^2+\mu\tau_{\max}).
\]
Using this choice in \eqref{eq:weighted-tilt}, with
$0<\tau\le\tau_{\max}$, gives
\[
 2a_0^{-2}|\nabla_\Sigma\tau|^2
 \le v^2=1+\alpha^{-2}|\nabla_\Sigma\tau|^2
 \le1+a_0^{-2}|\nabla_\Sigma\tau|^2.
\]
This implies $|\nabla_\Sigma\tau|^2\le a_0^2$ and $v^2\le2$,
contradicting the assumption $v>2$ at the interior maximum.
Since the logarithmic weight tends to $-\infty$ as $\tau\to0$,
we need only compare with the boundary maxima and points where
$v\le2$. The inequalities
$v\le e^{\operatorname{arcosh}v}\le2v$ then give
\eqref{eq:temporal-gradient}.

label: eq:causal-tangent-normalization
title: Proof
body_md:
Timelike displacement of a causal curve, with the displacement
chosen by a scalar differential equation, is used in the proof of
\cite{ChruscielGrant}. Here we need a displacement
that stays uniformly small along an inextendible curve while
producing infinite proper time. We construct it to show that
\eqref{eq:compact-proper-time} excludes a causal curve confined
to a compact set with no future endpoint in $\mathcal B$.
Suppose that $\gamma$ is such a curve.
Choose a $C^2$ future unit timelike field $V$ on a neighbourhood of
its compact closure, and use the Riemannian metric
$\mathbf g+2V^\flat\otimes V^\flat$ to measure tangent vectors.
Parametrize $\gamma$ so that its
almost-everywhere tangent $l$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:causal-tangent-normalization}
 \mathbf g(l,V)=-1,\qquad \mathbf g(l,l)\le0,\qquad
 |l|_{\mathbf g+2V^\flat\otimes V^\flat}^2\le2 .
\end{equation}
The parameter in \eqref{eq:causal-tangent-normalization}
ranges over $[0,\infty)$, since a finite range would give
finite Riemannian length in a compact set and hence an endpoint,
contrary to inextendibility. Put
\[
 b(s)=\mathbf g(l,\mathbf D_lV),\qquad |b|\le K,\qquad K\ge1.
\]
The bound follows from $|l|\le\sqrt2$ in
\eqref{eq:causal-tangent-normalization} and the bound for $\mathbf D V$
on the compact closure of $\gamma$.
Under a displacement $uV$, the linear change in the squared
norm of the tangent is $2bu-2u'$. The coefficient $b$ has no
sign, so a constant displacement does not suffice. We choose
$u'-bu=c_0u^2$ so that $2bu-2u'=-2c_0u^2$ dominates
the quadratic error. Infinite proper time will then follow from
$\int_0^\infty|u|\,\mathrm ds=\infty$, while a small bound for
$|u|$ keeps the displaced curve in a compact neighbourhood.
Put
\[
 \Lambda'(s)=\exp\left(\int_0^sb(t)\,\mathrm dt\right),
 \qquad \Lambda(s)=\int_0^s\Lambda'(t)\,\mathrm dt.
\]
The equation for the displacement becomes
\[
 \left(\frac{\Lambda'}u\right)'=-c_0\Lambda'.
\]
Thus $\Lambda'/u+c_0\Lambda$ is constant. Choosing its value
according to whether $\Lambda$ is bounded gives, for $c_0$
sufficiently large,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:causal-displacement}
 u(s)=
 \begin{cases}
 -\dfrac{\Lambda'(s)}{c_0(1+\Lambda(s))},
       &\Lambda(s)\longrightarrow\infty,\\[7pt]
 \dfrac{\Lambda'(s)}{c_0(\Lambda_\infty-\Lambda(s))},
       &\Lambda(s)\longrightarrow\Lambda_\infty<\infty .
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
The two choices in \eqref{eq:causal-displacement} satisfy,
almost everywhere,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Riccati}
 u'=b u+c_0u^2,\qquad
 |u|\le\frac K{c_0},\qquad |u'|\le2K|u|,
 \qquad \int_0^\infty|u|\,\mathrm ds=\infty .
\end{equation}
Indeed, in the first case
$\Lambda'\le1+K\Lambda\le K(1+\Lambda)$.
In the second case
\[
 \Lambda_\infty-\Lambda(s)
 =\int_s^\infty\Lambda'(t)\,\mathrm dt
 \ge\Lambda'(s)\int_s^\infty e^{-K(t-s)}\,\mathrm dt
 =\frac{\Lambda'(s)}K .
\]
Integrating \eqref{eq:causal-displacement} gives, in the two
cases respectively, $\int_0^s|u(t)|\,\mathrm dt$ equal to
\[
 c_0^{-1}\log(1+\Lambda(s))\qquad\text{and}\qquad
 c_0^{-1}\log[\Lambda_\infty/(\Lambda_\infty-\Lambda(s))].
\]

Choose $u_0>0$ and a compact neighbourhood $C'$ containing
$\Psi_{u,V}(\overline\gamma)$ for $|u|\le u_0$.
Set $\widetilde\gamma(s)=\Psi_{u(s),V}(\gamma(s))$.
For $c_0\ge K/u_0$, the bound $|u|\le K/c_0$ in
\eqref{eq:Riccati} keeps $\widetilde\gamma$ in $C'$.
Its tangent is
\[
 \dot{\widetilde\gamma}
       =\mathrm d\Psi_{u,V}(l+u'V).
\]
The $C^2$ bounds for $\mathbf g,V$ on $C'$ bound
$\mathcal L_V\mathbf g$ and $\mathcal L_V^2\mathbf g$ there.
Using $(\mathcal L_V\mathbf g)(l,l)=2b$ and
\eqref{eq:causal-tangent-normalization} gives the Taylor
expansions below, with remainder constants independent of
$s$ and $c_0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:flow-metric-expansion}
 \begin{aligned}
 (\Psi_{u,V}^*\mathbf g)(l,l)&=\mathbf g(l,l)+2b u+O(u^2),\\
 (\Psi_{u,V}^*\mathbf g)(l,V)&=-1+O(|u|),\\
 (\Psi_{u,V}^*\mathbf g)(V,V)&=-1.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Combining \eqref{eq:flow-metric-expansion} with the equation
for $u$ in \eqref{eq:Riccati} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:displaced-curve-norm}
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathbf g(\dot{\widetilde\gamma},\dot{\widetilde\gamma})
 &=\mathbf g(l,l)+2b u-2u'-(u')^2+O(u^2+|uu'|)\\
 &\le-2c_0u^2-(u')^2+O(u^2)
 \le-c_0u^2<0 .
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Here the bound $|u'|\le2K|u|$ in \eqref{eq:Riccati} makes
the remainder constant independent of $c_0$. To check that
the timelike displacement preserves the future orientation,
use the mixed term in \eqref{eq:flow-metric-expansion} to obtain
\[
 \mathbf g(\dot{\widetilde\gamma},V)
       =-1-u'+O(|u|)<-\tfrac12.
\]
Thus each finite segment of $\widetilde\gamma$ is future
timelike and satisfies the hypotheses of
\eqref{eq:compact-proper-time}. Indeed, its tangent is bounded,
and the positive minimum of $|u|$ on that interval makes
\eqref{eq:displaced-curve-norm} a uniform timelike bound.
But \eqref{eq:displaced-curve-norm} and \eqref{eq:Riccati}
give
\[
 L_\mathbf g(\widetilde\gamma|_{[0,S]})
       \ge\sqrt{c_0}\int_0^S|u|\,\mathrm ds
       \longrightarrow\infty .
\]
This is a contradiction. Time reversal excludes
past-inextendible causal curves confined to compact sets.

Having excluded future- and past-inextendible causal curves
in compact sets, we apply Beem's theorem to an open
$\mathcal O$ with $Q\Subset\mathcal O\Subset\mathcal B$.
The theorem makes $\mathcal O$ stably causal, meaning that
its cones can be widened while preserving
causality~\cite{MinguzziCausality}. It therefore admits a
smooth temporal function with past timelike
gradient~\cite{MinguzziCausality}.
